name: Late Holocene rainforest crisis opens a savanna corridor
what: A drier, more seasonal climate fragmented the Central African rainforest about 2,500 years ago, opening savanna patches along the Sangha River Interval.

name: Bantu-speaking farmers cross the Sangha River Interval
what: Farming communities speaking Bantu languages pushed south through the opened corridor toward the southern savannas.

name: Iron smelting in the Great Lakes region (Urewe)
what: Urewe-ware communities west of Lake Victoria were smelting iron by the mid-first millennium BCE.

name: Great Lakes Bantu speakers adopt grain and cattle from their neighbours
what: Ehret reads loanwords to show Mashariki Bantu speakers took sorghum, finger millet and cattle-keeping from Central Sudanic and Cushitic speakers.

name: Eastern Bantu speakers spread from the Great Lakes to the Indian Ocean
what: Within a few centuries, iron-using farmers reached the coast of East Africa and moved south through the woodlands.

name: Bantu-speaking farmers reach southern Africa
what: Early Iron Age farming villages with cattle and iron appear south of the Limpopo in the first half of the first millennium CE.

name: Bantu-speaking farmers mix with forager and herder populations
what: Genomes of living Bantu speakers carry ancestry from rainforest foragers, Khoe-San and East African herders picked up along the way.

name: Equatorial political tradition of house, village and district
what: Vansina reconstructs a shared Bantu political vocabulary: the big-man house, the village and the district, the seeds of later chiefdoms.

name: Cattle wealth on the Zimbabwe plateau
what: Large herds, moved seasonally between highveld and lowveld, were the everyday wealth of plateau elites.

name: Zimbabwe plateau gold and ivory flow to Sofala and Kilwa
what: Gold dust and ivory went down to the coast at Sofala and on to Kilwa, in exchange for glass beads, cloth and Chinese ceramics.

name: Great Enclosure built at Great Zimbabwe
what: The largest single precolonial stone structure south of the Sahara, with walls up to 11 m high, built of dressed granite without mortar.

name: Firewood, grazing and soils run down around Great Zimbabwe
what: A town of perhaps several thousand people and its cattle wore out the land within walking distance.

name: Gold trade shifts north to the Zambezi valley
what: The coastal trade moved toward Zambezi routes controlled by the Mutapa state.

name: Great Zimbabwe loses its primacy
what: The capital stopped being the centre of the plateau world, though people kept living there.

name: Power passes to Khami (Torwa) and Mutapa
what: Successor states in the southwest (Khami) and the north (Mutapa) carried on the Zimbabwe building tradition.

name: Settler myth of foreign builders becomes doctrine
what: Rhodes-sponsored writers credited Phoenicians, Sabaeans or Arabs with the ruins and cast Africans as mere labourers.

name: R. N. Hall strips Great Zimbabwe of its archaeological deposits
what: Hired to "clean" the site, Hall dug away metres of layered deposits he took for later African "debris".

name: Randall-MacIver dates the ruins to the African Middle Ages
what: The first trained archaeologist to dig there found only African material and a medieval date.

name: Caton-Thompson confirms an African origin
what: Sent by the British Association, she excavated undisturbed deposits and concluded the builders were Bantu-speaking Africans.

name: Rhodesian government pressures archaeologists over Great Zimbabwe
what: Under the settler regime, official guidebooks were made to hedge on who built the site; Peter Garlake left his post as Inspector of Monuments in 1970.

name: Independent Zimbabwe takes the ruins’ name
what: The new state named itself after the site and put the soapstone Zimbabwe Bird on its flag.

name: Bambuk and Bure goldfields worked by Mande miners
what: Alluvial gold washed and dug by village communities, many of them women, under their own chiefs.

name: Sunjata defeats Sumanguru at Kirina and founds Mali
what: The founding victory of the Mali empire, remembered in the griots’ Sunjata epic.

name: Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage passes through Cairo
what: Musa crossed the Sahara with a vast retinue and gave away so much gold that Cairo talked about it for a generation.

name: Gold loses value in Cairo after Musa’s visit
what: Al-ʿUmari reports that the gold price fell and had still not recovered twelve years later.

name: The Catalan Atlas pictures the king of Mali holding gold
what: Abraham Cresques’ Majorcan world map shows Musa enthroned with a gold nugget, the richest king in the land of the blacks.

name: Succession disputes and breakaways weaken Mali
what: Rival heirs, a weakened court and the breakaway of Songhay and Tuareg-held Timbuktu shrank the empire.

name: Europe’s fifteenth-century bullion famine
what: Mints across Europe ran short of gold and silver; John Day called it the great bullion famine.

name: Portuguese build São Jorge da Mina on the Gold Coast
what: A fortified trading post to buy Akan gold at the coast, bypassing the Saharan caravans.

name: Gold diverted from Saharan to Atlantic routes
what: A growing share of West African gold left by sea rather than by camel.

name: Brazilian sugar plantations turn to enslaved African labour
what: Bahia and Pernambuco became the first great plantation economy fed by the Atlantic trade.

name: Sugar revolution in Barbados and the English Caribbean
what: Planters switched from tobacco and indentured Europeans to sugar and enslaved Africans within a generation.

name: The Atlantic slave trade at its peak
what: In the last decades of the eighteenth century ships carried more captives across the Atlantic than in any other period.

name: Deaths on the Middle Passage
what: Of about 12.5 million people embarked, roughly 1.8 million died at sea, mostly of dysentery and fevers.

name: The illegal slave trade to Brazil and Cuba
what: After British abolition, millions more Africans were shipped, mainly to Brazil and Cuba.

name: Brazil ends its slave trade (Eusébio de Queirós law)
what: Under British naval pressure, Brazil outlawed the import of captives and enforced it.

name: Kongo’s civil wars after Mbwila
what: After the king died at Mbwila in 1665, rival houses fought for the throne for forty years and sold prisoners to the coast.

name: Kongo’s eighteenth-century wars send soldiers into the slave trade
what: Prisoners of Kongo’s succession wars, many of them trained soldiers, were sold to French ships bound for Saint-Domingue.

name: Dahomey conquers Ouidah
what: King Agaja’s army took the coastal slave port of Ouidah, giving Dahomey direct access to European buyers.

name: Raiding, kidnapping and judicial enslavement spread
what: Villages, neighbours and even kin turned on one another as captives became a currency.

name: Firearms imports to West Africa surge
what: Inikori counted hundreds of thousands of guns a year shipped from England to West Africa in the later eighteenth century.

name: West and West-Central Africa’s population stagnates
what: Manning’s demographic model has the population of the slave-exporting regions flat or falling while the rest of the world grew.

name: Slavery becomes a central institution inside Africa
what: Lovejoy’s transformation: slavery grew from a marginal status into a mode of production.

name: European cloth and metal imports compete with African crafts
what: Rodney argued imports stunted African manufacturing; Thornton replies that imports were a small supplement to strong local industries.

name: Droughts drive famine and enslavement in Angola
what: Joseph Miller links recurring droughts to famines in which people pawned or sold dependants and themselves.

name: Temperature shocks at African slave ports
what: Year-to-year swings in local temperature, which Fenske and Kala match to port-level export data.

name: Ethnic fragmentation in heavily raided regions
what: Raiding broke larger political units into small, mistrustful communities.

name: Low trust among groups most exposed to the slave trade
what: In the 2005 Afrobarometer, people whose ethnic groups lost more people to the trade trust relatives, neighbours and local government less.

name: Lower incomes today where slave exports were highest
what: Nunn finds the African countries that exported the most slaves are among the poorest today.

name: Industrial Revolution in Britain
what: Mechanised cotton spinning, coal and steam reshape the British economy.

name: British abolitionist mass petitioning
what: Hundreds of thousands signed petitions to Parliament against the slave trade, starting with Manchester in 1787.

name: Palm oil and groundnuts: “legitimate commerce”
what: West African exports shifted to vegetable oils for British soap, lubricants and candles.

name: Maize and cassava spread through Africa
what: American crops became staples across West and Central Africa.

name: The Sokoto jihad builds a slave-holding caliphate
what: Usman dan Fodio’s jihad created the Sokoto Caliphate, one of the largest slave societies of the nineteenth century.

name: Scramble for Africa
what: In about thirty years, European states claimed nearly the whole continent; in 1880 most of Africa was under African rule.

name: Egypt’s state bankruptcy and Anglo-French Dual Control
what: Khedive Ismail’s debts put Egypt’s finances under European commissioners.

name: ʿUrabi movement in Egypt
what: Army officers and notables led by Ahmad ʿUrabi challenged the khedive and European financial control.

name: Malaria and yellow fever keep Europeans to the coast
what: Curtin’s figures show European soldiers in West Africa dying at several hundred per thousand per year before quinine.

name: Quinine prophylaxis cuts European deaths in the tropics
what: Regular quinine doses, proven on the 1854 Niger expedition, cut white mortality sharply.

name: Breech-loaders and machine guns open a firepower gap
what: Repeating rifles and the Maxim gun gave small colonial columns overwhelming firepower.

name: British and French capital exports soar
what: Britain invested a huge share of its savings abroad, though mostly in the Americas, settler colonies and Europe, not tropical Africa.

name: Falling palm oil prices squeeze West African trade
what: Lower world prices for vegetable oils hurt African producers, rulers and European merchants alike: Hopkins’ crisis of adaptation.

name: Leopold II’s Congo Free State
what: A personal colony of the Belgian king, recognised by the powers in 1885.

name: The red rubber regime of forced collection
what: Quotas, hostage-taking and mutilation forced villagers to tap wild rubber.

name: Sleeping sickness epidemics in the Congo basin
what: Trypanosomiasis spread along newly busy rivers and caravan routes.

name: Population decline in the Congo Free State
what: Contemporaries saw villages emptied; the size of the loss is unknown and estimates run up to Hochschild’s disputed ten million.

name: Colonial borders split ethnic homelands
what: Lines drawn in European capitals cut across the homelands of many ethnic groups.

name: More conflict in partitioned homelands
what: Split ethnic homelands see more political violence and discrimination after independence.

name: Samori Touré resists the French conquest
what: The Wassoulou empire fought the French for sixteen years, moving its whole state east when pressed.

name: Maji Maji rising in German East Africa
what: A rebellion against forced cotton growing, united by a water medicine said to turn bullets to water.

name: Saint-Domingue becomes the richest plantation colony in the world
what: By 1789 the colony produced more sugar and coffee than any other, worked by about half a million enslaved people.

name: Most of Saint-Domingue’s enslaved are African-born
what: Because deaths outran births, imports kept the African-born, many from Kongo, a majority on the eve of revolution.

name: Maroon bands, Vodou and plantation networks
what: Runaway communities and religious gatherings linked plantations before 1791.

name: The August 1791 uprising in the Northern Plain
what: Tens of thousands of enslaved people burned the plantations of the richest plain in the Caribbean.

name: Sonthonax proclaims emancipation in the North
what: Facing invasion and revolt, the French commissioner freed the enslaved of the Northern Province in August 1793.

name: Toussaint Louverture governs Saint-Domingue
what: The former slave became general-in-chief and governor, and issued his own constitution in 1801.

name: Leclerc’s expedition to restore French control
what: Napoleon sent tens of thousands of troops; Toussaint was seized and deported to France.

name: Haiti declares independence
what: Dessalines declared the independence of Haiti at Gonaïves on 1 January 1804.

name: France sells Louisiana to the United States
what: With its Caribbean army dying, Napoleon gave up his American empire.

name: Cuban sugar boom on the ruins of Saint-Domingue
what: Cuban planters rushed into the market Saint-Domingue had left and imported Africans on a new scale.

name: France imposes a 150-million-franc indemnity on Haiti
what: Recognition came at gunpoint and at a price, later reduced to 90 million francs.

name: Haiti’s long fiscal drain
what: Payments on the indemnity and the loans raised to pay it ran for over a century.

name: Pétion aids Bolívar on condition of emancipation
what: Haiti gave Bolívar refuge, guns and ships; Bolívar promised to free slaves in the lands he liberated.

name: The Haitian Revolution is silenced
what: Trouillot: contemporaries found a slave revolution unthinkable, and later historians wrote it out of the age of revolutions.

name: The Taíno population of Hispaniola collapses
what: Within a generation of Columbus, the island’s Native population fell to a few thousand.

name: Encomienda and forced-labour grants
what: The crown granted settlers the labour of Native communities, first on Hispaniola, then on the mainland.

name: The New Laws restrict Native enslavement and encomienda
what: Charles V banned the enslavement of Native Americans and limited encomiendas, after Las Casas’ campaign.

name: Central Mexico loses about nine in ten people
what: Cook and Borah’s figures fall from about 25 million in 1518 to about 1 million by 1605.

name: Andean population falls steeply
what: Epidemics, war and forced labour cut Andean numbers by well over half within a century.

name: Sixteenth-century megadrought in Mexico
what: Tree rings record the worst droughts of the past 500 years, with severe episodes in the 1540s and 1570s.

name: Second great cocoliztli epidemic
what: A haemorrhagic fever that Acuna-Soto and colleagues estimate killed close to half of the Native population left in central Mexico.

name: De Soto’s entrada through the Southeast
what: Hernando de Soto’s army marched through the Mississippian chiefdoms, taking captives and supplies.

name: The Mississippian chiefdoms of the Southeast collapse
what: Mound centres were abandoned and survivors regrouped as new confederacies such as the Creek and Choctaw.

name: The Native slave trade of the colonial Southeast
what: English Carolina armed Native raiders to capture and sell other Native people.

name: Abandoned fields regrow across the Americas
what: Koch and colleagues estimate about 56 million hectares of farmland went back to forest and savanna.

name: The 1610 Orbis spike: a dip in atmospheric CO2
what: Antarctic ice cores (Law Dome) show CO2 falling about 7 to 10 ppm to a low around 1610.

name: Spanish steel, horses and guns reach Mexico
what: Cortés landed near Veracruz with about 500 men, 16 horses and a few cannon.

name: Tlaxcala allies with Cortés
what: After fighting the Spaniards, Tlaxcala’s leaders chose alliance against their old Mexica enemies and sent thousands of warriors.

name: The myth that the Mexica took Cortés for a god
what: Post-conquest writers spread the story that Moctezuma thought Cortés was the returning Quetzalcoatl.

name: Nahua city-states survive under Spanish rule
what: Altepetl kept their councils, lands and Nahuatl paperwork under new Spanish names.

name: Warmer centuries let Andean farming climb higher
what: Lake sediments near Cusco record warming and agroforestry that raised maize yields at altitude.

name: Inca storehouses and the mitʼa labour tax
what: The Inca state ran on rotating labour service and thousands of storehouses, not markets or money.

name: The Huascar-Atahualpa civil war
what: After Huayna Capac died in an epidemic, his sons fought for the throne; Atahualpa’s generals won just as Pizarro arrived.

name: Huanca, Cañari and other Andean peoples ally with the Spaniards
what: Peoples recently conquered by the Inca supplied the Spaniards with warriors, porters and food.

name: Taki Onqoy millenarian movement
what: Dancers possessed by the huacas preached that the Andean gods would destroy the Spaniards and their diseases.

name: Indigenous guayra wind furnaces smelt Potosí ore
what: Andean wind furnaces on the hillsides did the smelting in the first boom, and Native workers kept much of the silver.

name: Huancavelica mercury mine supplies Potosí
what: The mercury needed to amalgamate Potosí’s ore came from Huancavelica in the central Andes.

name: Viceroy Toledo organises the Potosí mita
what: Each year about 13,000 men from sixteen highland provinces were drafted to work at Potosí.

name: Potosí becomes one of the largest cities in the Americas
what: At 4,000 metres, the mining town grew to perhaps 100,000 people or more.

name: Mercury poisoning in the Andean mines
what: Miners and refiners breathed and absorbed mercury vapour; Huancavelica was called the mine of death.

name: American silver floods into Europe and Asia
what: Spanish America produced most of the world’s silver for two centuries.

name: European population recovers after the Black Death
what: More mouths and growing towns pushed up the price of food.

name: The European price revolution
what: Prices in Spain and across Europe rose several-fold over the sixteenth century.

name: Ming Single Whip reform puts taxes in silver
what: Ming China commuted land taxes and labour service into payments of silver.

name: Silver imports to China falter
what: Atwell argued that falling Japanese and American silver arrivals deepened the late Ming fiscal crisis.

name: Former mita districts are poorer today
what: Households inside the old mita catchment consume about 25 percent less than those just outside it.

name: Wet centuries fuel Maya growth
what: A Belize cave stalagmite records unusually high rainfall in the Early Classic.

name: A long drying trend after 660
what: Rainfall declined in steps, with severe droughts after 800.

name: Late Classic Maya lowland population peak
what: LiDAR suggests millions of people in the central lowlands, with dense farms, terraces and causeways.

name: Late Classic deforestation and soil erosion
what: Fields and lime-burning for plaster stripped forests and washed soil into lakes.

name: Escalating war among Maya kingdoms
what: Monuments record more conflicts in the Late Classic, and defensive walls go up.

name: The Petexbatún kingdom breaks apart in war
what: Dos Pilas was abandoned after 761 and its region fell into fortified fragments, decades before the droughts.

name: Divine kingship loses its hold
what: Holy lords who claimed to bring rain and victory stopped raising dated monuments.

name: Maya people regroup in the north and on the coasts
what: Southern cities emptied, but Maya people and polities carried on elsewhere, and millions of Maya live today.

name: A long lull in big Mississippi floods
what: Lake cores near Cahokia record few large floods for six centuries, so the floodplain could be farmed.

name: Maize farming intensifies in the American Bottom
what: Maize became a staple in the fertile floodplain around Cahokia.

name: Drought in the Cahokia region
what: Tree rings and lake sediments record drier growing seasons after the mid-1100s.

name: A major Mississippi flood hits the American Bottom
what: A large flood layer around 1200 marks the return of big floods.

name: Cahokia builds a palisade around its centre
what: A bastioned wall about 3 km long enclosed Monks Mound and the Grand Plaza, rebuilt several times.

name: Cahokia’s people disperse
what: The great town shrank through the 1200s and was largely empty by 1350.
